Xiaomi's Robot Shift and October Delivery Record Meet a Margin Test
sum: Xiaomi's Beijing car plant has become something of a showcase. Visitors attending the World Media Summit toured the facility this week, and Xinhua Silk Road is holding it up as a model of advanced manufacturing. More than 700 industrial robots work the line, backed by AI-driven quality checks. For anyone holding the stock, though, the interesting question isn't how the factory looks — it's whether the technology inside it eventually shows up in the earnings.

The scale is already there. Xiaomi had delivered more than 800,000 vehicles in total by the end of October. On Sunday, the company reported over 50,000 electric cars shipped for October 2026 alone — the highest monthly figure of the year, according to Reuters, though Xiaomi did not disclose an exact number. That delivery record is the clearest company-specific signal in the current news flow, but it measures volume, not profitability. A strong shipment number on its own says nothing about the profit contribution behind it.

On Tuesday, Xiaomi published footage of its CyberOne-02 humanoid robots sorting center-console trim panels. The trial ran across an eight-hour shift with two charging breaks. According to the company, the robots detected and corrected anomalies on their own and coordinated with the production control system. Xiaomi describes the exercise as a preliminary validation at a single workstation. For a proper economic assessment, details on the number of parts handled and the level of human intervention would matter.

That self-correction capability is the part worth watching. A robot earns its keep when it copes with deviations and keeps a process reliable. Xiaomi aims to integrate humanoid robots into its factories within five years, but the CyberOne-02 remains a prototype. The upside for shareholders is a long-term one — provided the tests turn into repeatable, economically viable applications. Charging breaks, meanwhile, are part of the operating arithmetic: their impact depends on how cleanly they can be scheduled into the production flow.
The financial backdrop sharpens the scrutiny. In the second quarter of 2026, the gross margin of the Smart EV, AI and other new initiatives segment fell to 19.2%, down from 26.4% a year earlier.

sum: The Hang Seng Index gave up most of a strong opening rally on Monday 12 October 2026 but still closed 59.85 points higher, as banks and NetEase offset a 5.55% drop in Xiaomi and weakness in Hong Kong's technology sector.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 24,271.20 on Monday 12 October 2026, up 59.85 points or 0.25% from Friday's close of 24,211.35. Full-day turnover on the main board was HK$162.6 billion. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index also rose 0.25% to 8,168.57, while the Hang Seng Tech Index fell 0.67% to 4,169.57.

The shape of the session told a more cautious story than the headline gain. The index opened sharply higher at 24,434.93 and touched an intraday high of 24,455.95 in the first few minutes of trading, helped by early buying in Alibaba and NetEase. It then slid steadily through the morning, dropped to a low of 24,193.30 shortly after the lunch break, briefly below Friday's close, and recovered in the afternoon to finish modestly positive.

Banks and insurers provided the main support. China Merchants Bank rose more than 3%, and financial heavyweights helped the index hold its gains while technology shares diverged. Investors in Hong Kong were also reacting to a Saturday meeting in Beijing at which China's securities regulator signalled fresh support for the domestic stock market, although that message landed far less convincingly on the mainland, where the SSE Composite fell 0.43%.

The opening strength reflected Wall Street's record-setting week. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq both posted record closes last week, and Hang Seng futures pointed to a firmer start before the bell. That early optimism faded as investors weighed the impact of higher global interest rates, oil prices near $106 a barrel and fresh Middle East tensions after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to regional market reports.

A sharp sell-off in South Korea also weighed on regional technology shares. Seoul's Kospi plunged 3.65% after Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies, known as CXMT, reported progress on a next-generation DRAM design. The news hit Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix and spilled over into chip and AI-related names across Asia.

Xiaomi's Record October Deliveries Collide With a Citi Profit Warning
sum: Xiaomi's auto unit has just posted its strongest month of 2026, but the timing of the announcement means equity investors never got to trade it in isolation. The October delivery figure — more than 50,000 vehicles — landed after Friday's close, a session in which the stock had already added 2.0%. The shares then jumped 6.2% as the new week's trading got under way.

That split reaction frames the central tension facing shareholders: booming vehicle demand on one side, deteriorating earnings expectations on the other. Citi is sticking with its Buy rating even as it models a markedly weaker quarterly result.

Cumulative deliveries from January through October 2026 reached roughly 336,490 units, according to Reuters. Against a full-year target of 550,000 vehicles, that leaves a substantial chunk of the plan crammed into November and December.

The autumn momentum is unmistakable. August brought higher volumes, September stepped up again, and October delivered the year's peak. Xiaomi did not break the latest month down by model, so which vehicles powered the surge remains an open question.

Through October, the company had covered about 61% of its annual goal. Media reports calculate that clearing the remaining distance would require average monthly deliveries of roughly 106,755 units in the final two months — more than double December 2025's previous monthly record of 50,212 vehicles. The October release, published only as a lower bound, also cannot yet be confirmed as a new all-time monthly high.
For the third quarter, Citi projects revenue of 104 billion yuan, an 8% decline year on year. The bank expects Xiaomi to report on 24 November 2026.
Adjusted net profit is forecast at 4.8 billion yuan — a 58% drop from a year earlier and 19% below consensus.

sum: Xiaomi Corp. is continuing its capital-return program with another share repurchase. On October 27, the company bought back about 2 million Class-B shares for roughly 50 million Hong Kong dollars, according to a Reuters report carried by TradingView News.

The transaction gives investors a concrete measure of Xiaomi's capital allocation rather than a new operating forecast. Shares bought under the program are intended for cancellation, which would reduce the number of shares in issue once completed. The repurchase price range reported for the October 27 transaction was 25.48 to 25.68 Hong Kong dollars per share.

The latest purchase follows earlier buybacks in October. Xiaomi's authorization allows the company to repurchase a much larger number of shares, but individual filings do not establish how quickly management will use the full mandate. For investors, the immediate effect is therefore limited to the shares actually acquired and the potential reduction in the share count after cancellation.

The buyback comes as Xiaomi's electric-vehicle business remains an important part of the investment case. Earlier company disclosures cited strong initial demand for the SkyNomad range, while analysts have continued to weigh vehicle growth against pressure in the smartphone business. The mix between higher-growth vehicle and connected-device activities and the more mature handset operation will remain central to earnings expectations.

Hang Seng Jumps to 24,211.35 as Xiaomi, Tencent and Internet Stocks Lead a Sharp Rebound in Hong Kong
sum: Hong Kong's benchmark erased Thursday's 1.4% loss as bargain hunters returned to beaten-down technology and financial stocks, with the Hang Seng Tech Index surging 3.1% from close to a two-year low.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 24,211.35 on Friday 9 October 2026, up 425.56 points or 1.79% from Thursday's close of 23,785.79. The index opened at 23,941.26, which also marked the session low, and never looked back. It climbed through the morning, extended its gains after the lunch break and reached a session high of 24,224.05 shortly after 2 p.m. local time before holding most of that advance into the close.

Market turnover was HK$209.2 billion. The Hang Seng Tech Index jumped 124 points, or 3.1%, to 4,197, although it remains close to a two-year low. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index added 137 points, or 1.7%, to 8,147. The rally left the Hang Seng up about 1% for the week.

Friday's gain was largely a rebound. On Thursday, the Hang Seng fell 1.4%, or 345 points, as a Wall Street sell-off and a sharp rise in US Treasury yields deepened fears of higher-for-longer interest rates. Technology shares led those losses, with Lenovo down 8.1%, SMIC down 6.7% and Kingboard Laminates down 6.4%. Investors returned on Friday to buy shares that had fallen hard over two sessions.

Easing geopolitical tension also helped. Oil prices fell after President Donald Trump said the United States would not attack Iran before the 3 November midterm elections, which reduced fears of a new energy shock. US stock futures rose, and Asian markets broadly recovered from early losses. Reports that OpenAI expects its annualised revenue to reach $70 billion or more by the end of the year also helped soothe nerves after Thursday's Financial Times report on the company's revenue rattled AI-linked stocks worldwide.

Xiaomi was the standout performer, surging about 9.7% to HK$25.84. The smartphone and electric-vehicle maker was boosted by strong demand for its new vehicles, with reports of more than 70,000 pre-orders for its latest model in its first 30 days. Short-video platform Kuaishou rose about 5.5% and Tencent gained about 3.3%, as internet companies led the market higher. Meituan and Alibaba also advanced.

Xiaomi's 800,000th Rollout Meets a EUR 24 Billion Bet — and a Share Price Still 56% Off Its Peak
sum: Xiaomi has now handed over more than 800,000 vehicles since deliveries began in April 2024, founder Lei Jun announced on Monday — a milestone reached in roughly 29 months. The company's automotive arm is scaling fast, with monthly shipments in August 2026 still running above 30,000 units. Yet none of that momentum has translated into relief for shareholders.

The product pipeline keeps widening. On 7 September, Xiaomi unveiled three new SUVs under its Sky Nomad banner — the N70 Pro, N70 Max and N90 Max — pushing the brand further upmarket. Days earlier, at IFA in Berlin, the group signed letters of intent with eight German dealer groups, among them Emil Frey Germany, Ernst Dello and Hahn Automobile, laying the groundwork for a European launch of its battery-electric cars in 2027 that will start in Germany. A separate agreement with the LUEG Mobility Group was also part of the 3 September package. The emphasis is shifting visibly: from pure domestic volume growth toward a genuinely global footprint.

Backing that ambition is a spending plan of more than EUR 24 billion for the years 2026 to 2030. The money is earmarked for research and development, with artificial intelligence, operating systems, semiconductors, intelligent vehicles, robotics and manufacturing technology as the priority fields. The scale of the program signals how determined Xiaomi is to reduce its dependence on outside suppliers.

The clearest expression of that goal is the Xring O3, a 3-nanometer chip developed entirely in-house. It already powers both the company's flagship foldable and the new Pad 9 Pro Max tablet. Taken together — chip design, vehicle manufacturing and a software ecosystem — the strategy is meant to transform Xiaomi from a smartphone maker into a broader technology group.

Second-quarter 2026 figures show both sides of that transition. The segment bundling electric vehicles, AI and other new initiatives lifted revenue 17.1% to roughly USD 3.7 billion, of which about USD 3.5 billion came from vehicles. The unit's operating loss, however, remained around USD 385 million — heavy investment in a business still deep in the red.
At group level, revenue slipped 6.1% year on year to USD 16.0 billion, though it edged past analyst forecasts.

sum: Xiaomi finds itself squeezed between two forces that rarely appear in the same sentence: a product pipeline running at full throttle and a regulatory cloud gathering over one of its most important overseas markets. The Chinese technology group is simultaneously pushing into premium hardware, laying groundwork for an eventual European car business, and absorbing the fallout from an Indian fraud referral that could complicate its expansion plans.

At the center of the current uncertainty is a recommendation from India's Serious Fraud Office, reported by Reuters on September 9, urging a detailed investigation into Xiaomi's local operations. The referral cites alleged irregularities in the company's business model as well as non-compliance with foreign investment regulations. Xiaomi responded defensively, stating it had not yet received any formal notice from the relevant authority. Even so, the development carries weight. India has served for years as the company's most significant growth engine for budget smartphones outside its home market, and any regulatory action there would strike at a core pillar of its international strategy.

While legal questions simmer, Xiaomi's hardware machine keeps rolling. On September 11, the company unveiled the REDMI Note 17 Pro Max 5G, a device built around a 9,210 mAh battery with a promised runtime of up to three days — a clear statement in the volume segment. The classic smartphone business faces saturated markets worldwide and fierce margin competition.

Higher up the price ladder, Xiaomi has spent the past two weeks rolling out new foldable models. That territory puts the company directly against established rivals Huawei and Apple.

sum: Xiaomi (1810.HK) is set to unveil its annual flagship smartphone. Chairman Lei Jun announced that the autumn product launch event will take place this Wednesday (September 23) at 7:00 p.m., where the Xiaomi 18 Pro series will be officially released alongside several other new tech products. President Lu Weibing teased on Weibo that the new device will be priced higher than its predecessor, while emphasizing that the increase is reasonable.

Lu Weibing said the Xiaomi 18 Pro series represents the largest upgrade in the company's history across four core areas—performance, secondary display, screen, and imaging—marking a "full evolution into the 2.0 era." The new phone will be the first to ship with the all-new Xiaomi HyperOS 4, and will feature a hardware-level privacy screen, a versatile rear secondary display, a flat unibody design, and ultra-thin 0.99mm bezels. The imaging system adopts a 2nm chip-based Leica dual 200-megapixel ultra-clear solution, continuing Xiaomi's spec-war approach to camera hardware.

Battery endurance is a key breakthrough for this generation. The Xiaomi 18 Pro packs a 7,000mAh Jinshajiang battery, while the Pro Max version pushes capacity to 8,500mAh, leveraging ultra-high silicon battery technology to set a new record for the series.

On the pricing question that has drawn the most outside attention, Lu Weibing did not shy away. The Xiaomi 17 Pro currently starts at CNY 5,699 (approximately $850), and he acknowledged that "the new phone will see a price increase, but I believe everyone will find it reasonable," hinting that the hike will reflect the extent of hardware upgrades.

Notably, the CNY 5,699 price point itself has already gone through one round of increases. When the Xiaomi 17 Pro launched in September 2025, it started at CNY 4,999. Xiaomi then adjusted official pricing across the board on September 1, raising each 17-series variant by CNY 600 to CNY 1,100 (approximately $90 to $160), with the top-tier 16GB+1TB configuration seeing a single adjustment of CNY 1,100. The real driver is memory, not cameras or batteries: Counterpoint Research noted that chipmakers are prioritizing production capacity for high-bandwidth memory needed in AI servers, squeezing supply of standard DRAM used in smartphones.

sum: BEIJING – Haidilao International Holding’s sudden slump after its co-founder sold about US$350 million (S$445 million) worth of shares is putting the spotlight on other stocks that may be vulnerable to similar selling.

Owners have a 90-day grace period ending on Oct 22 to settle what they owe without late-payment surcharges.

“Business owners will view the current period as a rare transitional phase, when conditions are likely to be most favourable, giving them an incentive to settle tax obligations sooner rather than later,” said Dong Yizhi, a lawyer at Joint-Win Partners, a Shanghai-based law firm.

That is drawing attention to other founder-controlled companies, including Li Ning, Xiaomi and Sunac China Holdings, where large stakes are held through offshore trust structures, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

sum: Xiaomi has been making some cool cars lately. Back in December 2023, the Chinese smartphone maker unveiled their first car, the Xiaomi SU7. I remember watching the livestream and the presentation was less of a car launch and more of a civilisational leap. Core technologies, a hyper-engine, a battery architecture that will redefine range, and a chassis so advanced that it would make the SU7 one of the fastest EVs around the Nurburgring track a few months down the line. Xiaomi’s automotive division has been talked-about a lot in the EV and the car world. Not necessarily for good things.

Now everything that we were told during the December 2023 showcase would have been great, if it weren’t for the keynote theatrics. Because one look at what’s actually bolted under the Xiaomi SU7 or any other subsequent car that they have launched so far, a very different picture forms, one that Xiaomi’s marketing department has been noticeably reluctant to paint. Let’s “brake” it down, shall we?

Apart from the car design looking like Xiaomi has taken notes (to put it politely) from Porsche and/ or McLaren, Xiaomi is sourcing batteries for its cars from Chinese manufacturers Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. (CATL) and BYD. The brakes are sourced from Brembo and the brake-by-wire and stability control systems are made by Bosch. The shock absorbers are supplied by ZF Friedrichshafen, air springs by Tuopu (Ningbo Tuopu Group), bearings by Schaeffler, tyres by Michelin and Pirelli, front subframes by Gestamp, rear subframes by Benteler, steering by Nexteer, and so on. This is the documented, publicly reported supply chain of the Xiaomi SU7. The same car that Xiaomi markets as “A revolutionary EV experience.”
Now sourcing components is not an unusual thing in the automotive industry. What is unusual is the gap between how Xiaomi talks about these components and what it actually did to create them.

items.t: Q2 Smartphone Landscape Shifts: Huawei and Apple Gain Share, Xiaomi Shipments Plunge Over 20%
sum: In the second quarter of 2026, China's smartphone market underwent a significant reshuffle. The combined share of Huawei and Apple jumped from 33% a year ago to 41%, while Xiaomi's shipments fell more than 20%—the steepest decline among the six major vendors. The wave of price increases and soaring memory chip costs are redrawing the competitive map.

Counterpoint data shows that in Q2 2026, Huawei held a 23% share of China's smartphone market, with Apple in second place at 18%, followed by vivo, OPPO, Xiaomi, and Honor at 16%, 15%, 12%, and 11% respectively. A year earlier, Huawei's share was 18% and Apple's was 15%. The sharp rise in their combined share means the remaining vendors are being squeezed into an even tighter space.
Source: Counterpoint Research, China smartphone market share quarterly tracker (updated August 2026)

Xiaomi's Q2 shipment decline exceeded 20%, the largest drop among the six mainstream vendors. According to Omdia, Xiaomi's shipments in the China market fell 21%. Xiaomi cited two reasons in its earnings report: first, it proactively adjusted its product mix and reduced mid-to-low-end models; second, rising prices for memory and other key components dragged down global demand.

A source in the handset industry said vendors, worried about further memory price increases, have been procuring components ahead of schedule and pushing more phones into distribution channels. Channel inventory stocking propped up Q2 shipment figures, so shipment data looked better than actual end-user sales. Counterpoint data shows Q2 vendor shipments fell only 1%, while end-user sell-through declined by double digits year-over-year. Shipments measure phones sent into channels by vendors; sell-through measures phones actually purchased by consumers.

Huawei's ability to delay price increases into Q2 is attributed by Omdia to vertical integration and supply chain control. But pricing only explains part of the gains. The 5 percentage points Huawei picked up also stem from the restoration of supply for mass-market products. Over the past two years, Huawei's handset recovery relied mainly on the Mate and Pura series, while volume-driving lines like the Enjoy (Changxiang) series remained constrained by chip and component supply.

OPPO has responded to weakening entry-level demand by emphasizing smartphones with better cameras, AI features, larger batteries and higher memory configurations. The Reno16 family — including the Reno16 Pro 5G, Reno16 5G and Reno16 F 5G — supports this move into higher-value price segments.

The company is also using zero-interest instalments of up to 24 months, loyalty points and periodic online sales to reduce the immediate cost for Malaysian buyers without depending entirely on permanent price reductions.
Samsung and Xiaomi each captured 16 percent of Malaysia’s smartphone shipments, placing them three percentage points behind OPPO.

sum: Xiaomi Corporation (OTC:XIACF) is no longer content to compete through hardware design and pricing alone. The Chinese smartphone maker has unveiled the Xring O3, which is the second generation of its proprietary handset processor, as it seeks greater control over the technology powering its devices.

The strategy could improve product differentiation and bolster Xiaomi's negotiating position with outside chip suppliers, all the while supporting its expansion into premium smartphones. However, the investment comes as rising component costs and weakening global handset demand are already pressuring the company's core business. Let's dive deeper into it.

Developing processors internally could give Xiaomi greater control over several features that influence the smartphone experience. A system-on-chip integrates computing, graphics, artificial intelligence processing, and imaging functions, allowing the company to optimize important capabilities around its own hardware and software. Xiaomi launched its first proprietary smartphone processor, the Xring O1, in 2025. During its latest earnings call, the company said cumulative shipments of O1-powered smartphones, tablets, and watches had surpassed one million units. Although Reuters' sources estimated that only approximately 150,000 of those shipments were smartphones, the broader total shows Xiaomi has already deployed the technology across multiple product categories.

The O3 could also support Xiaomi's push into more expensive devices. According to two people familiar with the plans, TSMC will manufacture the processor using its 3-nanometre technology. sum: The stock has clawed back 11 percent in a week, closing Friday at EUR 3.16 with a 3.9 percent daily gain. On the surface, that looks like a vote of confidence. But the more telling number sits in the company's capital-returns program: Xiaomi has already spent roughly HKD 11.7 billion on share repurchases in 2026, surpassing its entire buyback volume for the prior year. Management is putting money where its mouth is on valuation — even as the market waits to see whether the electric-vehicle division can deliver on a promise that keeps getting harder to keep.

The SU7 sedan crossed 500,000 cumulative deliveries on Monday, a figure reached over 28.5 months since launch. That is a genuine production achievement, evidence that the assembly lines are running at meaningful scale. Yet July's monthly figure of 31,267 vehicles tells a more complicated story — it came in below the prior month, a sequential dip that chips away at the narrative of an uninterrupted ramp.

The official 2026 target remains 550,000 units. To hit it, Xiaomi would need to average roughly 67,000 deliveries per month for the rest of the year — more than double July's pace. That gap is the crux of the tension: the milestone is real, but the math required to close out the year is steep.

Guosen Securities nonetheless sees the EV arm posting a 20 percent gross margin for full-year 2026, building on the 19.2 percent margin reported in the vehicle business. The firm's case rests on an improving product mix and economies of scale — a view that treats the current margin trajectory as a floor, not a ceiling.

Tuesday's quarterly report laid the pressure bare. Revenue came in at CNY 108.9 billion against a consensus of CNY 112.2 billion, while adjusted net profit landed at CNY 6.2 billion — a figure that marked a sharp decline. Reuters framed the miss as evidence that memory-chip pricing is compressing margins in the smartphone segment, though it also signaled the pressure could ease in the second half.

items.t: Xiaomi's Two Bets: A Phone Business Retrenching, an EV Business Accelerating
sum: The market's reaction to Xiaomi's latest quarterly report looks, on the surface, like a paradox. Net profit down more than a fifth, smartphone shipments off by over a quarter, and yet the stock has climbed steadily since the numbers landed last Tuesday. The explanation lies less in the headline figures than in what management says comes next.

President William Lu has declared the worst of the smartphone downturn over. The surge in memory-chip prices that has squeezed margins across the electronics industry is now decelerating, with further relief expected in the second half of the year. That framing reframes the narrative: not a demand problem, but a cost problem that is gradually resolving itself.

The second-quarter numbers show a company that has chosen margin over volume. Smartphone shipments fell 26.5 percent to 31.2 million units, yet the average selling price jumped 25.9 percent to 1,351 yuan. Revenue from the segment still slipped 7.5 percent to 42.1 billion yuan, but the strategic intent is clear — competing on premium devices rather than chasing market share in a saturated market burdened by expensive components.

Nomura, which reaffirmed its "Neutral" rating on Wednesday, attributed the revenue beat specifically to that ASP uplift and stronger IoT sales. The gross margin of 19.8 percent came in below the 20.4 percent consensus, but investors largely shrugged — an acceptance that a transition phase carries a cost as long as the trajectory holds.

Meanwhile, the electric vehicle business is expanding with an intensity that evokes Xiaomi's early smartphone ascent. Deliveries reached 104,199 units in the second quarter, up 28.2 percent year on year, with segment revenue climbing 15.9 percent to 23.9 billion yuan. The division still operates at a loss of 2.6 billion yuan, but management has raised its full-year delivery target to 550,000 vehicles — a significant step up from the 410,000 originally planned for 2025.

That target revision signals confidence that the EV operation can eventually rein in losses and become a core pillar of the group. The operating deficit of roughly 385 million US dollars in the segment is, in this view, the price of admission rather than a warning sign.

items.t: Xiaomi's Stock Defies a 42% Profit Collapse — Here's What Investors Are Actually Buying
sum: The arithmetic looks brutal on paper. Xiaomi's adjusted net income fell 42.6 percent year-on-year to 6.2 billion yuan in the second quarter, while revenue slipped 6.1 percent to 108.9 billion yuan. Yet the stock is climbing, closing Thursday at 3.05 euros and posting a 6.8 percent weekly gain. On a seven-day stretch, the advance reaches 10 percent, with a single session jump of 3.3 percent to 3.15 euros.
That disconnect between the income statement and the share price tells the real story: investors are pricing Xiaomi's future bets, not its current phone business.

The smartphone division remains the company's biggest headache. Segment revenue contracted 7.5 percent to 42.1 billion yuan as global shipments fell to 31.2 million units, a 26.3 percent drop from a year earlier. Gross margin in the handset business compressed to 8.5 percent, squeezed by persistently elevated memory-chip costs.

But there's a counter-narrative buried in those numbers. Xiaomi's average selling price jumped 25.9 percent year-on-year to 1,351 yuan — a record, according to CFO William Lu. The company is selling fewer phones but charging more for them. Whether that premiumization strategy can permanently offset the memory-cost burden is the central question hanging over the recovery.

The market share picture is mixed. Xiaomi held onto third place globally with an 11.5 percent share, trailing Samsung at 22.3 percent and Apple at 20.3 percent — its 24th consecutive quarter in the top three. But at home, the erosion is starker: shipments in mainland China fell to 8.4 million units, with market share dropping from 16.8 percent to 14.2 percent.

The optimists point to a rapidly diversifying growth engine. Xiaomi's electric vehicle business delivered 104,199 cars in the second quarter, marking its sixth consecutive year-on-year improvement. The flagship SU7 became the best-selling pure electric sedan above 200,000 RMB in the first half. The company's IoT and lifestyle segment posted a 20.1 percent margin, while internet services reached an eye-popping 76.8 percent.

Artificial intelligence adds to the momentum. Xiaomi's in-house language model, MiMo V2.5, topped the global open-source ranking in August by core volume, with usage multiplying more than sixfold in two months.
